questions.q: What does 'Lock sessions to the IP address from which they originated' protect against?
options: It encrypts all data at rest automatically
It is unrelated to session security
It prevents users from ever logging in twice
A stolen session token/cookie being reused from a different network
questions.explain: Pinning a session to its originating IP means a stolen session identifier can't simply be replayed from an attacker's own network — it has to match the IP that created the session.

options: Increasing a session's security level mid-session (e.g., prompting for MFA) without requiring a full re-login, before allowing a High-Assurance-gated action
A type of OAuth scope
A method for bulk-deactivating users
Logging out and logging back in every hour automatically
questions.explain: Step-up authentication lets a session that started at Standard security level be elevated to High Assurance mid-session — typically via an MFA prompt — right before a sensitive, High-Assurance-gated action is attempted.

questions.q: Why should refresh tokens be treated as more sensitive than access tokens?
options: There is no meaningful difference in sensitivity
Refresh tokens are actually less sensitive since they can't be used directly
A leaked refresh token lets an attacker mint new access tokens indefinitely, unlike a leaked short-lived access token
Refresh tokens expire within seconds, making them low-risk
questions.explain: Because refresh tokens are long-lived and can generate fresh access tokens repeatedly, a leaked refresh token has a much larger and longer-lasting blast radius than a leaked, short-lived access token.

questions.q: Why might deactivating a user's Salesforce login not be sufficient during offboarding?
options: Deactivation automatically revokes every token system-wide
This scenario can never actually occur in Salesforce
Deactivation is always fully sufficient and nothing else is needed
Outstanding OAuth tokens or connected app authorizations issued to that user may still be valid and usable for API access unless explicitly revoked
questions.explain: Deactivating a user doesn't automatically guarantee every previously issued OAuth token or connected-app authorization is invalidated — these need to be explicitly reviewed and revoked as part of a thorough offboarding process.

questions.q: Why does the lesson connect token scope (from Lesson 5) to token-handling discipline?
options: A leaked token's potential damage (its 'blast radius') is proportional to the scope it was issued with, so narrow scopes limit the consequences of any token leak
Scope only matters for SAML assertions, not OAuth tokens
Wider scopes always expire faster, mitigating their risk
Scope and token handling are unrelated topics
questions.explain: A token scoped narrowly (e.g., read-only on one object) causes limited damage if leaked, while a broadly scoped token (like 'full' access) causes much greater damage — which is why minimal scoping and careful token handling are two sides of the same discipline.
